turns.user: why do interviewers ask 'tell me about yourself' first, whats the point
turns.assistant: It's mostly a warm-up and a filter. It gives the interviewer a quick way to see how you communicate and what you think matters about your background, without having to read your whole resume again. It also lets them pick follow-up questions based on what you highlight. And it gives you a chance to set the narrative, so it's less about your life story and more about why you're a good fit for the job.

turns.user: so what should i actually say, like how long
turns.assistant: About 60 to 90 seconds. A simple structure: present (what you're doing now, like your major and any projects or internships), past (one or two experiences that prepared you for this role), and future (why this role and company interest you). Skip childhood and hobbies unless relevant. Keep the focus on things related to the job.

turns.user: why do they care about the 'future' part
turns.assistant: It tells them whether your goals match what the job can offer. If you say you're interested in data work and the role is data analysis, that suggests motivation and that you'll stay engaged. It also shows you know something about the company and haven't just sent out random applications. Employers prefer candidates who have a reason for choosing them.

turns.user: and the 'greatest weakness' question? why do they ask that
turns.assistant: They want to see self-awareness and how you handle your own gaps. Nobody expects a perfect candidate, and what matters is whether you recognize a real weakness and are doing something about it. A good answer picks a genuine but not critical weakness, like difficulty delegating or public speaking, and explains the steps you've taken to improve. Avoid fake answers like 'I work too hard,' which interviewers hear constantly.

turns.user: I'm a freelance designer, 31, sit at a desk all day and have been wanting to start lifting properly. I've got maybe 3 days a week, 60 minutes, and a regular gym membership with full equipment. I've never followed a program. I'm trying to decide between Starting Strength, a PPL split, and a full-body 3x/week program like GZCLP. Which one suits me?
turns.assistant:
For a complete beginner with 3 days a week, I'd rule out PPL first, because it's designed for 5 to 6 days a week. Running it on 3 days means each muscle is trained about once a week, which is less efficient.

That leaves Starting Strength and GZCLP, both full-body, 3 days. Starting Strength is the simplest: two alternating workouts of squat, bench or overhead press, and deadlift or power clean, with linear weight increases. GZCLP is a bit more flexible, with more accessory work, and handles stalls better. For you, either would work. If you want the simplest start, pick Starting Strength.

turns.user: I do like the simplicity. But I'm a bit worried about getting bored with only 3 lifts, and my shoulders get tight from computer work.
turns.assistant:
That's a fair point on both. GZCLP might suit you better then. It uses the same main lifts, but each session also includes accessory exercises like rows, face pulls, and lat pulldowns, which are good for the upper back and shoulder issues that come from desk work. You get more variety within the structure.

You can also add a few things to Starting Strength, like face pulls and band pull-aparts for 2 sets at the end, but then you are basically building your own version of GZCLP.

turns.user: OK, so GZCLP. How long does a session take? I only have 60 minutes including warmups.
turns.assistant:
A typical GZCLP session runs 60 to 75 minutes. Tier 1 (main lift, 5 sets of 3) takes about 20 minutes, Tier 2 (a second lift, 3 sets of 10) about 15 minutes, and Tier 3 (accessory, 3 sets of 15+) another 10 to 15. With warm-ups and rest periods it can go over an hour at the start.

To fit 60 minutes: rest 2 to 3 minutes between heavy sets, 60 to 90 seconds for accessories, do only 1 or 2 accessories, and warm up with just a few ramp-up sets. Over time you'll get faster.

turns.user: What about the weights? I don't know where to start for squats, for example.
turns.assistant: Start light and learn the movement. Do the bar alone (20 kg / 45 lb) for a few sets of 5, then add weight in small steps until the bar speed slows slightly but form stays good. Pick a starting weight that you could do about 8 to 10 times, but you are only doing 3 per set, which leaves lots of room. For most beginners this is 30 to 50 kg for squats. It's easier to move up than to recover from starting too heavy. In the first 2 weeks, focus on form and consider having a trainer check your squat and deadlift.

turns.user: That makes sense. Should I be eating differently? I'm not trying to bulk, just get stronger and maybe look less like a desk goblin.
turns.assistant: As a beginner you can get stronger and add a bit of muscle without a big diet change, if you eat enough protein and don't eat far below maintenance. A target of about 1.6 to 2.0 g of protein per kg of body weight a day (so for 70 kg, around 110 to 140 g) is plenty. Keep your calories around maintenance, and a small surplus isn't needed. Sleep matters too, 7+ hours. If you also want to lose a bit of fat, a modest deficit works at the start, but keep protein high.

turns.user: Great, thanks. And how long before I see a change?
turns.assistant: Strength comes first: you'll likely add weight to the bar every session for the first 4 to 8 weeks, since much of that is your nervous system learning the lifts. Visible muscle changes take longer, generally 8 to 12 weeks of consistent training and enough protein, and people around you tend to notice about the 3 month mark. Posture and shoulder comfort can improve sooner, within a few weeks, as the back exercises kick in. Take a few photos and note your lifts now, since the day-to-day change is hard to see.
